text_blocks.snippet: Type 2 diabetes is diagnosed using specific blood tests that measure your blood glucose or average blood sugar levels over time.
snippet_highlighted_words: using specific blood tests that measure your blood glucose or average blood sugar levels over time

text_blocks.snippet: According to guidelines from the American Diabetes Association, type 2 diabetes is diagnosed if you meet any of the following thresholds:

list.snippet: Hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c): 6.5% or higher (measures average blood sugar over the past 2 to 3 months; does not require fasting).
Fasting Plasma Glucose (FPG): 126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L) or higher (measured after at least 8 hours of no caloric intake).
Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT): 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) or higher measured 2 hours after drinking a 75-gram glucose solution.
Random Plasma Glucose: 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) or higher in a person who has classic symptoms of high blood sugar (such as frequent urination, extreme thirst, or unexplained weight loss).

Repeat Testing: Unless you have unmistakable symptoms of high blood sugar or a very high blood glucose level, doctors typically confirm the diagnosis by repeating the same test or running a second different test on a separate day.

Prediabetes Range: Blood sugar levels that are elevated but below the threshold for diabetes indicate prediabetes: an A1c of 5.7% to 6.4%, a fasting blood sugar of 100 to 125 mg/dL, or a 2-hour OGTT result of 140 to 199 mg/dL.

text_blocks.snippet: You can learn more about screening guidelines and patient resources through MedlinePlus or review clinical overviews via the JAMA Network.
